You are a creative technologist researching AWARD-WINNING web animation and interaction techniques, to inform a premium, highly-engaging (not AI-slop) homepage for "Nxeon" (a cloud hosting platform: VPS, web hosting, game servers, AI-assisted one-command deploy, a multi-agent "Matrix" build feature, free migration). The site is Next.js + React + Tailwind; we can use Canvas, WebGL/Three.js, SVG, and scroll libraries.

Use WebSearch/WebFetch. Research and catalog, with SPECIFICS and how-to-implement notes:
- Scroll-driven storytelling techniques: sticky/pinned sections, scroll-scrubbed animations, horizontal scroll, parallax done tastefully, section-by-section "scenes." Reference real examples (Apple product pages, Stripe, Linear, Igloo/Awwwards winners) and the modern implementation approach (CSS scroll-driven animations / animation-timeline, IntersectionObserver, GSAP ScrollTrigger, Framer Motion useScroll, Lenis smooth scroll).
- Canvas/WebGL hero effects that feel premium and perform at 60fps: particle/node fields, shader gradients, dot/grid fields reacting to cursor, generative backgrounds. When to use canvas vs WebGL vs CSS.
- Signature "wow" interactive moments: typing terminals, live product simulations, magnetic buttons, custom cursors, marquees, number counters, morphing SVG, draw-on-scroll SVG.
- Texture/depth tricks that de-genericize: film grain/noise overlays, dithering, subtle blur/glass, glow discipline, color grading.
- Performance + accessibility guardrails: prefers-reduced-motion, mobile fallbacks, avoiding jank, lazy-init heavy effects.

Then produce:
1. A ranked shortlist of ~8 techniques that would make Nxeon's site feel high-budget and memorable, each with a concrete implementation note (which API/library, rough approach).
2. Specifically: the best way to build (a) a "Matrix" multi-agent build visualization and (b) a website-migration animation (files/db/dns/ssl flowing from an old host into Nxeon) so they look premium, not clip-arty.
3. What to AVOID (animation clichés that read as templated/AI).

Be thorough and specific. Return a detailed structured report with implementation guidance.

I've completed the web search for CSS scroll-driven animations. Here's a summary of what I found:

## Overview

The CSS Scroll Timeline API is revolutionizing how we build interactive web experiences by allowing animations to be directly linked to scroll progress. The CSS scroll-driven animations spec introduces two new timeline functions (scroll() and view()), a new property (animation-range), and support for named timelines (scroll-timeline and view-timeline).

## Timeline Functions

The two main functions are:

- **scroll()**: The scroll() function creates a scroll progress timeline that's tied to the scroll position of a container, whereas view() creates a view progress timeline that's based on the visibility of an element within its container.

- **view()**: The CSS animation-timeline property accepts a view() function which, in turn, returns a timeline of how much of an element is visible in the part of a scroll container that's viewable, and view() runs animations based on the visibility of the animated element within a scrollport.

## Browser Support

Chrome 115 shipped the initial implementation in July 2023, and the spec has since reached stable support across all major browsers. However, Firefox added support in late 2025, which means it's finally safe to consider for production with a graceful fallback.

## Key Implementation Considerations

Do not set animation-duration — scroll position replaces time as the driver. Additionally, @supports rules can be used for CSS feature detection and providing fallbacks for unsupported browsers.

Based on the search results, here's what the current best practices are for scroll animation in 2025:

## GSAP ScrollTrigger vs Lenis

Lenis is a lightweight scroll smoother that lets you keep your native DOM structure and plays well with ScrollTrigger—you sync their scroll positions and get a natural, modern feel. Using Lenis with ScrollTrigger provides a smooth scroll experience without redesigning your layout around a tool's expectations.

GSAP's ScrollTrigger is the industry standard for scroll animations, and pairing it with Lenis is a match made in heaven.

## ScrollTrigger vs ScrollSmoother

When ScrollSmoother proved difficult with complex layouts, switching back to ScrollTrigger with fixed-position elements gave back control but cost the smoothness. This is where Lenis becomes valuable as a lightweight alternative.

## Framer Motion Integration

Choose Framer Motion (Motion) if you're building a React/Next.js app and most of your animation is component state, enter/exit transitions, layout shifts, and gestures. Note that in February 2025 Framer Motion was renamed Motion and the recommended import is now motion/react.

## 2025 Updates

In April 2025, Webflow made GSAP 100% free, including every plugin that used to be paid (SplitText, MorphSVG, ScrollSmoother, and more).

The consensus for 2025 appears to be: use GSAP ScrollTrigger + Lenis for complex scroll animations, and Framer Motion for component-level React animations.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about magnetic buttons, custom cursors, and premium web techniques:

## Magnetic Buttons & Custom Cursors

Magnetic Cursor makes UI elements (buttons, links) subtly move toward cursor as it approaches, creating magnetic attraction effect using JavaScript to calculate distance and translate elements. This modern UI interaction is commonly used on premium landing pages, product websites, and developer or designer portfolios.

## Implementation Techniques

**With Framer Motion:** The Magnetic Buttons template is a focused interaction primitive that tracks the cursor position via React pointer events, computes an offset based on how close the cursor is to the button's repel zone, and applies that offset as a transform through Framer Motion spring physics. A Lerp utility smooths each frame of cursor tracking so the pull feels physical rather than instantaneous.

**Vanilla JavaScript:** A magnetic hover effect can be built using only vanilla JavaScript and CSS transforms, offering a lightweight, easy-to-control implementation optimized for smooth performance without relying on external libraries.

## Noise & Effects

For creating a magnetic noisy circle cursor for navigation elements, Paper.js can be used with Simplex Noise.

## Custom Cursor Customization

Magnetic effects apply a CSS transform: translate() pull to matched elements as the cursor enters their activation radius, with the transform resetting when the cursor leaves. Parameters include strength, radius, and ease factors for controlling the magnetic effect behavior.

## Limitations

Mobile support is not optimized out of the box — touch events have a different model than pointer events, so the magnetic effect should be gated behind a hover media query before deploying to mobile audiences.

## Performance & 60fps Target

To achieve smooth 60fps performance, target under 100 draw calls. GPU-based particle systems run at 60fps with a million points while CPU-based approaches choke at ten thousand.

## GPGPU (General-Purpose GPU Computing)

GPGPU stands for General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units—a way of using the GPU to process data rather than rendering pixels, great for when you need to do the same complex calculation thousands of times. Use compute shaders for particle systems and physics.

## Instancing & Draw Call Optimization

Use InstancedMesh for repeated objects like particles. The most common issues are too many draw calls (solved by instancing and batching), unoptimized assets, and memory leaks.

## Cursor Interaction

When you click and drag, particles can be pushed away from the cursor, then spring back to their original positions when released. A more efficient way to introduce cursor interaction would be to do it in the shader by passing the cursor's position as a uniform and displacing particles based on their distance from it.

## Shader-Based Rendering

Every particle is a vertex; pre-allocate a Float32Array and upload it once—the GPU owns it after that, so you never touch it from JavaScript each frame.

Based on the search results, here's what the web resources reveal about `prefers-reduced-motion` accessibility best practices for web animation, mobile considerations, and performance:

## Core Accessibility Principle

prefers-reduced-motion is a media query that can be used in CSS to detect whether the user has requested reduced motion on their device or browser. Vestibular disorders affect more than 70 million people, and animations can trigger discomfort for those with vestibular motion disorders, with animations such as scaling or panning large objects being vestibular motion triggers.

## Implementation Best Practices

Always respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, as some users experience motion sickness or vestibular disorders from animations, with implementations providing alternative animations or instant transitions for users with reduced motion preference.

Most animations, especially decorative effects such as fades, slides, parallax, or hover transitions can simply be removed for people who prefer reduced motion, or alternatively, providing a static alternative to the animation.

## Mobile and Performance Considerations

When implementing parallax carefully, subtle movements (20-30% speed difference) avoid motion sickness, test on mobile (parallax can feel awkward on touch devices), ensure content readability, and provide fallback for users preferring reduced motion.

If animations perform poorly, reduce animated elements, simplify effects, use simpler timing functions, or consider removing animations on lower-powered devices using JavaScript device detection or CSS media queries.

## Code Example

A practical example uses @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to remove animations and provide instant visual states.

# Award-Winning Web Animation Techniques for the Nxeon Homepage — Research & Implementation Playbook

Research synthesized from CSS-Tricks, WebKit, Codrops, Three.js Journey, GSAP, Motion.dev, Awwwards, and the Stripe/Phaser gradient deconstructions (sources at the end). Everything below is tuned for a Next.js + React + Tailwind stack.

---

## Part 0 — The stack decision (read first)

Pick a small, coherent toolchain rather than piling on libraries. The 2025/26 award-site consensus:

- **Lenis** (`lenis`, from darkroomengineering) for smooth scroll — lightweight, keeps native DOM, syncs cleanly into ScrollTrigger. This is the single biggest "feels expensive" upgrade and it's ~2kb.
- **GSAP + ScrollTrigger** for scroll-scrubbed timelines, pinning, horizontal scroll. As of April 2025 **GSAP is 100% free including SplitText, MorphSVG, ScrollSmoother** (Webflow acquisition). This removes the old reason to avoid it.
- **Motion** (formerly Framer Motion; import from `motion/react` since Feb 2025) for React component-level work: enter/exit, layout transitions, gestures, `useScroll`/`useTransform`, spring physics for magnetic elements. Use it for anything tied to component state.
- **Three.js** (or **OGL** — much smaller, ~50kb — if you only need a shader plane/particles) for WebGL hero and heavy generative work.
- **CSS scroll-driven animations** (`animation-timeline: scroll()/view()`) for *cheap, JS-free* reveals and progress effects. Now cross-browser as of late 2025 (Firefox landed it); still gate behind `@supports (animation-timeline: view())` with an IntersectionObserver fallback.

Rule of thumb: **CSS/IntersectionObserver for reveals, GSAP+Lenis for scrubbed scenes, Motion for interactive components, WebGL only for the hero and the two signature set-pieces.** Don't run Lenis *and* ScrollSmoother — pick Lenis.

---

## Part 1 — Technique catalog (with how-to)

### A. Scroll-driven storytelling

**1. Sticky/pinned "scenes."** The Apple product-page pattern: a section is pinned to the viewport while its internal content advances as you scroll. Implementation: `ScrollTrigger` with `pin: true` and `scrub: true` (or `scrub: 1` for a smoothed 1s catch-up). Each scene is a GSAP timeline; scroll distance = pin duration via `end: "+=2000"`. Keep pinned sections to 2–4 total; more feels like a tunnel.

**2. Scroll-scrubbed animation.** Progress (0→1) drives properties instead of time. In React/Motion: `const { scrollYProgress } = useScroll({ target, offset: ["start end", "end start"] })` then `useTransform(scrollYProgress, [0,1], [0,-200])`. In GSAP: `scrub`. The Apple "AirPods explode into parts as you scroll" effect is a scrubbed image sequence — 100–200 pre-rendered frames drawn to a `<canvas>` indexed by scroll progress (this is how Apple actually does it; it's a `drawImage` per frame, not video).

**3. Horizontal scroll section.** Pin a section, then translate an inner track on X by scrubbed scroll: `gsap.to(track, { x: () => -(track.scrollWidth - innerWidth), scrollTrigger: { pin, scrub, end: () => "+=" + track.scrollWidth } })`. Great for a "your stack, one command" step sequence. Always provide a vertical-stack fallback on mobile and for reduced-motion.

**4. Parallax — tastefully.** Keep layer speed deltas at **20–30% max**; anything more induces motion sickness and reads cheap. Move background layers slower than foreground via `useTransform`/`y`. Prefer `transform: translate3d` (compositor-only) — never animate `top`/`margin`.

**5. Draw-on-scroll SVG.** Animate `stroke-dashoffset` from `pathLength` down to 0 as scroll progresses — perfect for the migration "pipe/flow" lines and connector paths. GSAP: `DrawSVGPlugin` (now free) or manual `stroke-dashoffset` with `scrub`. Pure CSS version: `stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1; animation-timeline: view()`.

**6. CSS-only reveals (the cheap win).** For fade/slide-up-on-enter, skip JS entirely:
```css
@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  .reveal { animation: rise linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: entry 10% cover 30%; }
}
@keyframes rise { from { opacity:0; translate:0 40px } to { opacity:1; translate:0 0 } }
```
Fallback: IntersectionObserver adding an `.in` class. This offloads work to the compositor and runs when JS is busy.

### B. Canvas / WebGL hero effects (60fps discipline)

**When to use what:**
- **CSS gradients/conic-gradient + blur** — for a simple animated aurora. Zero JS, cheapest. Good default.
- **Canvas 2D** — particle/node constellation *up to a few thousand points*; connecting-lines "network" effect. CPU-bound; fine for ~500–2000 nodes.
- **WebGL (shader plane)** — flowing mesh gradients, dot fields, anything per-pixel or >10k particles. GPU-bound, scales to a million points at 60fps.

**7. Shader mesh gradient (Stripe-style).** The signature "expensive SaaS" look. Technique deconstructed: a fullscreen fragment shader using **Fractal Brownian Motion — multiple octaves of Simplex noise** with varying lacunarity/persistence, coordinates modulated by `sin()/cos()` with a time uniform so it flows. Colors *blend* (not linear-lerp) for rich highlights/shadows. Stripe's whole effect is ~10kb ("minigl"). Nxeon move: use a **dark** palette (deep indigo/violet → cyan accents) and clip the canvas container with `transform: skewY(-8deg); overflow:hidden` for the sharp diagonal edge — Stripe fakes the angle in CSS, the canvas stays a plain rectangle.

**8. Interactive dot/node field reacting to cursor.** Do the interaction **in the shader**, not JS: pass `uMouse` as a uniform and displace each point by its distance from the cursor (`push away, spring back`). This is the Codrops "Interactive Particles" / Three.js-Journey "particles cursor" pattern. Pre-allocate one `Float32Array` of positions, upload once, let the GPU own it — never rebuild the buffer per frame. Use `THREE.Points` with a custom shader material, or `InstancedMesh` for shaped particles. Target **<100 draw calls**. A grid/dot field that gently repels around the cursor reads as "alive" without being noisy — ideal for the hero behind the headline.

**9. Generative background (GPGPU flow field).** For the highest tier, a GPGPU flow-field (positions computed in a fragment shader ping-pong texture) gives fluid, organic particle motion — the Codrops "dreamy particle effect." Heavy; only if you want a true centerpiece and you lazy-init it.

### C. Signature "wow" interactive moments

**10. Typing terminal.** The most on-brand element for a "one-command deploy" product. Build a fake terminal that types `nxeon deploy` char-by-char, shows a spinner, streams log lines, then a green success. Implement with a small state machine + `requestAnimationFrame` (not `setInterval`) or a typing lib; add a blinking caret, monospace font, and realistic latency jitter (randomize per-char delay 20–90ms so it doesn't feel robotic). Loop it. This alone communicates the whole product.

**11. Magnetic buttons.** On pointer-move within a radius, translate the button toward the cursor by a lerped offset; reset on leave. Motion version: track pointer via React events, compute offset, apply through a **spring** (`useSpring`) so it feels physical, with a `lerp` per frame. **Gate behind `@media (hover:hover)`** — touch has no hover, so disable on mobile. Keep strength subtle (max ~0.3× distance).

**12. Custom cursor.** A lerped follower dot that scales/changes on hover targets (the Codrops custom-cursor pattern). Use `mix-blend-mode: difference` for a cursor that reads on any background. Always keep the real cursor as fallback and disable on touch. Don't overdo — one tasteful state change on interactive elements.

**13. Number counters.** Count up stats ("99.99% uptime", "12s to deploy", "3,400 servers migrated") when they scroll into view. Motion's `useInView` + animated value, or GSAP `to({val:0}, {val:target, snap:1, onUpdate})`. Ease-out so it decelerates into the final number.

**14. Marquee.** Infinite logo/feature ticker via duplicated track + `translateX(-50%)` loop; pause on hover. Keep it slow. Use for trust logos or feature keywords, not everywhere.

**15. Morphing SVG.** `MorphSVGPlugin` (now free) to morph one icon path into another (e.g., a generic "server" morphing into the Nxeon mark) — great for a logo intro or feature-icon transitions.

### D. Texture & depth (de-generic-izing)

**16. Film grain / noise overlay.** The single cheapest "this isn't a template" trick. A fixed full-screen overlay with a tiling noise PNG (or an SVG `feTurbulence` `<filter>`) at `opacity: 0.03–0.06`, `mix-blend-mode: overlay`, `pointer-events:none`. Optional very slow animated jitter. Kills flat digital emptiness in dark UIs.

**17. Dithering / gradient banding fix.** Add a tiny amount of noise *inside* your shader/gradient (`+ (rand(uv)-0.5)/255`) to break up banding on large dark gradients — banding is the #1 tell of an amateur WebGL gradient.

**18. Glass / subtle blur.** `backdrop-filter: blur()` on floating nav/cards, but *discipline*: one blur layer, thin border (`1px rgba(255,255,255,0.08)`), subtle inner highlight. Overuse = generic glassmorphism.

**19. Glow discipline.** Accent glow via layered `box-shadow`/`filter: drop-shadow` in the brand accent, only on 1–2 focal elements (CTA, active terminal line). Restraint is what separates premium from gamer-RGB.

**20. Color grading.** Constrain to a tight palette (1 base dark, 2 accents). Add a faint vignette (radial gradient overlay, darker edges). This unifies disparate sections.

---

## Part 2 — The two signature set-pieces

### (a) "Matrix" multi-agent build visualization

Goal: convey *many AI agents collaborating to build your deploy* — should feel like a living system, not clip-art robots.

**Recommended build: SVG + Canvas hybrid, not literal Matrix rain.** Avoid the green-katakana cliché entirely (it's the #1 AI-slop tell). Instead visualize a **node graph of agents lighting up and passing work.**

Concrete approach:
- **Layout:** a central "orchestrator" node with 5–8 satellite agent nodes ("Frontend", "DB", "DNS", "Tests", "Deploy"…), arranged in an orbit/DAG. Use SVG for the nodes/labels (crisp text, easy hover) over a Canvas/WebGL layer for the ambient particle field behind.
- **Animation:** work "packets" travel along the connector paths between nodes — animate a small glowing dot along each SVG path using `offset-path: path(...)` + `offset-distance` 0→100% (CSS motion path), or GSAP `MotionPathPlugin`. Stagger them so the graph pulses continuously.
- **Draw-on:** connector lines draw in via `stroke-dashoffset` when the section enters view (scrubbed), so the network "assembles."
- **State:** each node cycles states (idle → working with a pulsing ring/spinner → done with a check), driven by a lightweight JS state machine on a timeline. Tie a **live log/terminal** beside it that streams the corresponding lines ("agent:db provisioning Postgres… ✓") so the graph and text reinforce each other.
- **Ambient field:** behind it, a dim WebGL dot field (technique #8) drifting slowly, subtly reacting to cursor — gives depth without stealing focus.
- **Premium tell:** monochrome + one accent, thin 1px lines, soft glow only on the *active* node and the moving packet, grain overlay on top. Everything eased (no linear), slight scale-pop on state change.

**Why this beats "Matrix rain":** it's *diegetic* — it literally shows the product's value (parallel agents building your app), it's legible, and orbit-of-nodes with traveling packets is a Stripe/Vercel-tier idiom rather than a screensaver.

### (b) Website-migration animation (files / DB / DNS / SSL → Nxeon)

Goal: show assets flowing *out of an old host* and *into Nxeon*, safely and completely.

**Recommended build: SVG scene + scrubbed GSAP timeline, packets on motion paths.**
- **Two anchors:** left = a dimmed, generic "Old Host" server card (desaturated, slightly lower); right = a bright, glowing "Nxeon" card. Curved connector "pipes" (SVG Bézier paths) arc from old to new.
- **Four labeled streams** flow along the pipes as distinct packet types with their own icon + color: **Files** (document glyph), **Database** (cylinder), **DNS** (globe/record), **SSL** (padlock). Animate each as a dot traveling the path via `offset-path`/`MotionPathPlugin`, staggered and looping.
- **Draw-on-scroll:** the pipes draw from old→new via `stroke-dashoffset` as the user scrolls (scrubbed), so migration visibly *progresses* with the scroll. A progress meter ("Migrating… 78%") + counter ties to `scrollYProgress`.
- **Arrival feedback:** when a packet reaches the Nxeon card, a small ripple/pulse and the card gains a check next to that stream (Files ✓, DB ✓, DNS ✓, SSL ✓). SSL arrives last and the padlock "closes" (small morph) → conveys "secured, done."
- **The old host** gradually desaturates/dims to near-empty as streams drain; **Nxeon** brightens and its glow intensifies — a clear before/after energy transfer.
- **Texture:** grain overlay, thin lines, glow only on active packets and the destination. Everything eased-in-out.

**Why premium, not clip-arty:** it's a single coherent scene with consistent iconography and physics, driven by scroll so the *user* performs the migration; the color-drain/brighten narrative reads instantly; no spinning gears or generic "loading" tropes.

For both: build a **reduced-motion static version** — the graph/scene rendered in its final "done" state with all checks green and a caption, no motion.

---

## Part 3 — Ranked shortlist: 8 techniques to make Nxeon feel high-budget

1. **Lenis smooth scroll (site-wide).** Biggest perceived-quality jump for least effort. `new Lenis()` + rAF loop; sync to ScrollTrigger via `lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update)`. ~2kb.
2. **WebGL shader hero gradient (Stripe-style FBM + Simplex noise), dark palette, skewed clip.** The "expensive SaaS" signature. Use OGL for a light footprint; add in-shader dithering to kill banding.
3. **Typing terminal for one-command deploy.** rAF state machine, jittered latency, streaming logs, green success. Most on-brand single element on the page.
4. **Cursor-reactive WebGL dot/node field behind the hero.** Displacement in-shader via `uMouse` uniform; `THREE.Points`, buffer uploaded once, <100 draw calls.
5. **Pinned scrubbed "scenes" for the 3–4 core features.** GSAP ScrollTrigger `pin + scrub`; each feature a mini-timeline. Include the two set-pieces above as two of the scenes.
6. **Film grain + vignette + glow discipline (global texture layer).** Fixed noise overlay at 3–6% opacity, `mix-blend-mode:overlay`; tight palette, one accent, restrained glow. De-templates everything.
7. **Magnetic CTAs + tasteful custom cursor.** Motion spring physics, gated behind `@media (hover:hover)`; blend-mode cursor. Subtle strength only.
8. **Scroll-into-view number counters + draw-on-scroll connector SVGs.** `useInView` counters for stats; `stroke-dashoffset` scrub for the migration pipes and agent-graph edges — cheap, high-impact, reinforces the set-pieces.

(Reveals via CSS `animation-timeline: view()` with IntersectionObserver fallback underpin all of it for free.)

---

## Part 4 — Performance & accessibility guardrails (non-negotiable)

- **`prefers-reduced-motion`:** Respect it globally. Provide a *static final-state* alternative, not just "remove." Vestibular disorders affect 70M+ people; parallax/scale/pan are triggers. Kill parallax, scrubbing, magnetic, and cursor effects; keep instant opacity states. Do it in both CSS (`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`) and JS (`matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')`) before initializing GSAP/WebGL.
- **Lazy-init heavy effects.** Don't boot WebGL until the canvas is near-viewport (IntersectionObserver) and after first paint. Pause `requestAnimationFrame` when the section/tab isn't visible (`document.hidden`, IntersectionObserver). This protects LCP/INP and battery.
- **Mobile fallbacks.** Detect low-power/touch: swap horizontal-scroll → vertical stack, WebGL particle field → static CSS gradient or a single low-res still, disable magnetic/custom cursor. Cap devicePixelRatio at ~1.5–2 for shaders. Reduce particle counts on mobile.
- **Compositor-only animation.** Only animate `transform`/`opacity` (and `filter` sparingly). Never `top`/`left`/`width`/`margin` in animations. Add `will-change` narrowly and remove it after.
- **60fps discipline for WebGL:** one buffer uploaded once, interaction in-shader via uniforms, `InstancedMesh`/`Points`, <100 draw calls, cap DPR, no per-frame allocations.
- **Don't run two scroll systems.** Lenis *or* ScrollSmoother, never both. One rAF loop for everything you can.
- **Test INP.** Heavy scroll listeners cause jank; scrub through GSAP/Lenis (which batch on rAF) rather than raw `scroll` handlers.

---

## Part 5 — Avoid (reads as templated / AI-slop)

- **Literal green "Matrix" katakana rain.** The #1 cliché; replace with the node-graph approach above.
- **Rainbow/neon everything and gamer-RGB glow.** Undisciplined glow screams template. One accent, focal glow only.
- **Generic purple blob mesh gradient with no grain** → banding + "every AI landing page." If you use a mesh gradient, dither it, darken it, skew-clip it, and pair it with grain.
- **Everything fading-and-sliding-up on scroll, all identical, all `ease` linear.** Vary reveals, stagger, ease-out; not every element needs to animate.
- **Excessive parallax / >30% layer deltas** — motion sickness + amateur.
- **Over-blurred glassmorphism cards stacked everywhere.**
- **Spinning gears, generic "loading" clip-art, robot mascots** for the AI/agent story — use diegetic system visuals instead.
- **Slow, mandatory intro/preloader animations** that block content — award juries and users both hate them; if you preload WebGL, let content be usable underneath.
- **Autoplaying full-screen video hero** as a crutch for having no real interaction.
- **Custom cursor that lags or hides the real one on mobile.** Always fallback + `hover:hover` gate.
- **Marquees and counters everywhere.** One of each, purposeful.

---

## Key sources
- WebKit: [Guide to scroll-driven animations with CSS](https://webkit.org/blog/17101/a-guide-to-scroll-driven-animations-with-just-css/) · CSS-Tricks: [Scroll-based animations in full view()](https://css-tricks.com/creating-scroll-based-animations-in-full-view/)
